citations.quote: Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: Choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ of $V$ by [F1], allowing $r=0$, and set $p=\sum_{j=1}^r\langle f,e_j\rangle e_j$. For each $\ell$, orthonormality gives $\langle f-p,e_\ell\rangle=\langle f,e_\ell\rangle-\sum_{j=1}^r\langle f,e_j\rangle\langle e_j,e_\ell\rangle=0$; since the basis spans $V$, $f-p$ is orthogonal to $V$.

For any $v\in V$, $p-v\in V$ and $f-p$ is orthogonal to $V$. Expanding the squared norm of $f-v=(f-p)+(p-v)$ therefore gives $\|f-v\|^2=\|f-p\|^2+\|p-v\|^2$. If $q\in V$ also has $f-q$ orthogonal to $V$, then $p-q=(f-q)-(f-p)$ lies in $V^\perp$ and in $V$, hence $\|p-q\|^2=0$ and $p=q$. Taking $v=0$ gives the stated norm identity.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

derivations.claim: For every $z\in\mathbb R^n$, $z^TAz=z^TKz+z^TRz\ge0$ by [F1], and $A$ is symmetric. Hence $A$ is a nonnegative endomorphism of the finite-dimensional real inner-product space $\mathbb R^n$.

By [F2], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j\ge0$. In this basis, $A$ is invertible exactly when no $\lambda_j$ is zero, while $z^TAz=\sum_j\lambda_j c_j^2$ for $z=\sum_j c_je_j$ is positive for every nonzero $z$ exactly when all $\lambda_j>0$. Thus $A$ is invertible if and only if it is positive definite.

In the same basis, $A^*A=A^2$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_j^2$. By [F4], its unique nonnegative square root has eigenvalues $\lambda_j$, so [F3] says the singular values of $A$ are precisely these $\lambda_j$. By [F5], the SVD has full rank exactly when all $n$ singular values are positive, which is exactly the invertibility condition in step 2.1.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Assume the Axiom of Choice The Axiom of Choice. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ Stochastic processes and their finite-dimensional distributions
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_jX_{t_j}
$$
has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of Multivariate normal law, including singular covariance. Indeed, that definition says
exactly that every scalar projection of the vector is normal. This also covers
repeated times, zero coefficients, and singular covariance matrices; no
distinct-time convention is needed for this definition.

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

where $n,p\ge1$ and repeated indices are allowed. Write
$f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$, $f_{X_*}=(f_{x_j^*})_{j=1}^p$,

symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\epsilon$. Assume the
observed covariance $C=K_{XX}+R$ is positive definite. Then a version of the

$$N_p\!\left(m_*+K_{*X}C^{-1}(y-m_X),\;K_{**}-K_{*X}C^{-1}K_{X*}\right).$$
The displayed conditional covariance is positive semidefinite and may be
singular; $K_{XX}$ and $K_{**}$ may also be singular. If a prediction-noise

the conditional mean is unchanged and
$R_*$ is added to the conditional covariance. The displayed kernel is a
version defined at every $y$; conditional-law versions are determined only

For computation, the occurrences of $C^{-1}v$ mean solving $Cu=v$. Since
$C$ is positive definite, its Cholesky factorization and forward/back
substitution evaluate these solves without forming $C^{-1}$.

In the finite observation model, let $K=K_{XX}$ and let $R$ be symmetric and
positive semidefinite. Then $A=K+R$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
Its ordinary inverse exists if and only if $A$ is positive definite,
equivalently if and only if all singular values of $A$ are positive. Thus the

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Thus the projection definition [F3] gives $Y\sim N_n(m_X,A_X)$.

Apply [F5] to the law from step 1.1, using the hypothesis $A_X\succ0$. Its density at $y$ is $(2\pi)^{-n/2}\det(A_X)^{-1/2}\exp\!\bigl(-\frac12(y-m_X)^TA_X^{-1}(y-m_X)\bigr)$. This is positive, so taking its logarithm and expanding products gives the displayed formula.

It is bounded because $\lVert Sh\rVert_2^2=\sum_i|\langle h,k_{x_i}\rangle_H|^2\le\lVert h\rVert_H^2\sum_i\lVert k_{x_i}\rVert_H^2$. The reproducing identities then give its adjoint $S^*\beta=\sum_i\beta_i k_{x_i}$, since $\langle Sh,\beta\rangle=\sum_i\beta_i\langle h,k_{x_i}\rangle_H=\langle h,S^*\beta\rangle_H$. Consequently $SS^*=K$ and $V=\operatorname{ran}(S^*)=\operatorname{span}\{k_{x_i}:1\le i\le n\}$.

For every $c\in\mathbb R^n$, $c^T(K+\sigma^2I_n)c=c^TKc+\sigma^2\lVert c\rVert^2\ge\sigma^2\lVert c\rVert^2$, because $K$ is a Gram matrix of the positive-semidefinite kernel. Hence $A=K+\sigma^2I_n$ is positive definite and, by [F6], its ordinary inverse exists. Put $r=y-m_X$, $\alpha=A^{-1}r$, and $h_0=S^*\alpha$.

Write $g=m+h$, so $J(m+h)=\lVert r-Sh\rVert^2+\sigma^2\lVert h\rVert_H^2$. By [F2], each $h$ decomposes uniquely as $p+q$ with $p\in V$ and $q\perp V$. Then $Sq=0$ by the reproducing identities, and $\lVert p+q\rVert_H^2=\lVert p\rVert_H^2+\lVert q\rVert_H^2$. Thus $J(m+p+q)=J(m+p)+\sigma^2\lVert q\rVert_H^2$, so minimization reduces to $V$.

Let $B=K^{1/2}$ be supplied by [F3], and define $C:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\oplus\mathbb R^n$ by $C\beta=(K\beta,\sigma B\beta)$. For $h=S^*\beta$, its objective is $\lVert C\beta-(r,0)\rVert^2$, because $Sh=K\beta$ and $\lVert S^*\beta\rVert_H^2=\beta^TK\beta=\lVert B\beta\rVert^2$. The normal equation is $C^*C\beta=C^*(r,0)$, that is $(K^2+\sigma^2K)\beta=Kr$. Our $\alpha$ satisfies it because $(K^2+\sigma^2K)\alpha=K(K+\sigma^2I_n)\alpha=Kr$. Therefore [F4] makes $h_0$ a minimizer on $V$.

For any $d\in H$, $Sh_0-r=K\alpha-r=-\sigma^2\alpha$ and $S^*(Sh_0-r)=-\sigma^2h_0$. Expanding both squared norms and using the adjoint identity gives $J(m+h_0+d)-J(m+h_0)=\lVert Sd\rVert^2+\sigma^2\lVert d\rVert_H^2$. This is nonnegative and is zero only for $d=0$, so the minimizer is unique on all of $H$, not just on $V$.

The minimizing function is $g_*=m+h_0=m+\sum_i\alpha_i k_{x_i}$, and $S h_0=K\alpha$, giving the displayed evaluation vector. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $f=(f_t)_{t\in\mathcal X}$ be a
real Gaussian process with mean $m$ and symmetric positive-semidefinite
covariance kernel $k$, and let $X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n\in\mathcal X^n$ with $n\ge1$.
For independent observation noise $\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ with symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariance $R$, set $Y=f_X+\varepsilon$,
$m_X=(m(x_i))$, $K_{XX}=(k(x_i,x_j))$, and $A_X=K_{XX}+R$. Suppose
$A_X$ is positive definite. Define the log marginal likelihood at
$y\in\mathbb R^n$ as the logarithm of the Lebesgue density of $Y$ at $y$
under this prior-predictive model. Then $Y\sim N_n(m_X,A_X)$ and
$$\log p(y\mid X,m,k,R)=-\frac12(y-m_X)^TA_X^{-1}(y-m_X)-\frac12\log\det(A_X)-\frac n2\log(2\pi).$$
This formula is asserted only for the nonsingular observed-covariance case
$A_X\succ0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Assume the Axiom of Choice The Axiom of Choice. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ Stochastic processes and their finite-dimensional distributions
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_jX_{t_j}
$$
has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of Multivariate normal law, including singular covariance. Indeed, that definition says
exactly that every scalar projection of the vector is normal. This also covers
repeated times, zero coefficients, and singular covariance matrices; no
distinct-time convention is needed for this definition.

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian positive definite and let
$A=LL^*$ be its Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal.

1. For every right-hand side $b\in\mathbb C^n$, the system $Ax=b$ is solved by
   first solving $Ly=b$ and then solving $L^*x=y$.
2. The two triangular solves cost $2n^2+O(n)$ scalar operations altogether, and
   the dense Cholesky factorisation costs
   $$\frac{1}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   scalar operations, compared with
   $$\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(n^2)$$
   for dense LU factorisation without exploiting symmetry.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, $m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, and
$k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ a symmetric kernel whose every
finite Gram quadratic form on points of $\mathcal X$ is nonnegative. Let
$f=(f_t)_{t\in\mathcal X}$ be the canonical Gaussian process with
$m(t)=\mathbb E[f_t]$ and
$k(s,t)=\mathbb E[(f_s-m(s))(f_t-m(t))]$. For finite ordered lists
$A=(a_i)_{i=1}^r$ and $B=(b_j)_{j=1}^s$ in $\mathcal X$, set
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))$; repetitions are allowed. Take
$X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n\in\mathcal X^n$ and
$X_*=(x_j^*)_{j=1}^p\in\mathcal X^p$ with $n,p\ge1$, and write
$m_X=(m(x_i))$, $m_*=(m(x_j^*))$, $f_X=(f_{x_i})$, and
$f_*=(f_{x_j^*})$. Let $\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of $f$,
where $R$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\varepsilon$ and
$A_X=K_{XX}+R$. Suppose $A_X$ is positive definite. Then for every
$y\in\mathbb R^n$ the conditional law of $f_*$ given $Y=y$ has mean
$$m_*+K_{*X}A_X^{-1}(y-m_X)$$
and covariance
$$K_{**}-K_{*X}A_X^{-1}K_{X*}.$$
This covariance is positive semidefinite and may be singular. If
$\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ is independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$, where
$R_*$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, then the conditional law of
$f_*+\eta_*$ has the same mean and covariance with $R_*$ added. The displayed
kernel is defined for every $y$, although regular conditional versions are
determined only $P_Y$-almost surely.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

derivations.claim: Cholesky factorization costs $n^3/3+O(n^2)$ by [F5]. For one test point, the posterior variance formula requires solving $A_Xu=k_{X*}$ and forming $k_{**}-k_{*X}u$. Factoring $A_X=L L^T$ reduces this to two triangular solves, each with $O(n^2)$ cost by [F5], followed by an $O(n)$ inner product. Therefore the variance calculation after factorization is $O(n^2)$.

The spectral norm of $A_\epsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\epsilon)$ is $1$, its smallest singular value is $\epsilon$, and therefore its spectral condition number is $1/\epsilon$. The perturbation $E=\operatorname{diag}(0,-\epsilon)$ has norm $\epsilon$, so $\lVert E\rVert_2/\lVert A_\epsilon\rVert_2=\epsilon$, while $A_\epsilon+E=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ is singular. Thus operation counts alone do not control sensitivity to finite-precision perturbations near singularity.

The scalar kernel $k_\theta(t,t)=\theta$ is positive semidefinite for $\theta\ge0$, and the observed covariance is $A_\theta=1+\theta>0$. Apply [F1] with $m=0$ and $y=0$ to get $L(\theta)=\tfrac12\log(1+\theta)+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)$. Differentiating twice gives $L''(\theta)=-1/(2(1+\theta)^2)<0$ for every $\theta>0$, so this negative log marginal likelihood is not convex on its parameter domain.

Write $\sigma(z)=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}$; then $0<\sigma(z)<1$ for all $z$, so $\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(z)\sigma(z)\,dz$ is finite and positive. The logistic posterior is therefore a positive density whose log, up to an additive constant, is $q(z)=-z^2/2-\log(1+e^{-z})$. Differentiation gives $q'''(z)=-\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))(1-2\sigma(z))$. At $z=\log 3$ this equals $3/32\ne0$. A positive density on all of $\mathbb R$ cannot be a degenerate Gaussian; every nondegenerate univariate Gaussian log density is quadratic and has third derivative zero, so this posterior is not Gaussian.

Since $0<\Phi(z)<1$ for all $z$, the probit posterior normalizer $\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(z)\Phi(z)\,dz$ is finite and positive. Its positive log density, up to an additive constant, is $q(z)=-z^2/2+\log\Phi(z)$. Put $h=\phi/\Phi$ and $c=h(0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$. Since $(\log\Phi)'=h$ and $h'=-zh-h^2$, differentiation yields $(\log\Phi)'''(0)=h''(0)=-c+2c^3=c(4/\pi-1)\ne0$; the last inequality uses $\pi<4$. A positive density on all of $\mathbb R$ cannot be a degenerate Gaussian; every nondegenerate univariate Gaussian log density is quadratic and has third derivative zero, so this posterior is not Gaussian.

Let $D=\{t_i:1\le i\le r\}$ for any finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_r\in[0,1]$. The equality kernel has Gram form $\sum_{t\in D}(\sum_{i:t_i=t}a_i)^2\ge0$. Therefore it is positive semidefinite, and by [A1, F2] it defines a cylinder-space Gaussian process with standard normal coordinates and covariance $1_{s=t}$.

For any finite list of distinct inputs in $[0,1]$, [F3] gives a centered Gaussian vector with covariance identity. By [F4] its characteristic function is $\exp(-\tfrac12\sum_i u_i^2)$, which factors into the univariate standard-normal characteristic functions; uniqueness therefore gives independent standard-normal coordinates.

Let $q_j=1/(j+2)$. If a continuous modification $G$ existed, the equalities $G_{q_j}=f_{q_j}$ for all $j$ and $G_0=f_0$ would hold simultaneously almost surely, since there are countably many coordinates. Let $E_0=\{|f_0|<1\}$, which has positive probability, and $E_j=\{|f_{q_j}|>2\}$, each of probability $p>0$ by [F2]. The finite-coordinate independence from step 2.1 gives $\Pr(E_0\cap\bigcap_{j=N}^M E_j^c)=\Pr(E_0)(1-p)^{M-N+1}$. By [F7], letting $M\to\infty$ gives $\Pr(E_0\cap\bigcap_{j=N}^\infty E_j^c)=0$ for each $N$; the countable union over $N$ then shows $E_0$ and infinitely many $E_j$ occur together with probability $\Pr(E_0)>0$. On that event $|G_0|<1$ while $|G_{q_j}|>2$ infinitely often, contradicting continuity at $0$. No continuous modification exists.

The scope distinction in [F6] concerns a Gaussian observation likelihood; the explicit logistic and probit posterior calculations in steps 1.4 and 1.5 have nonzero third derivatives and are not Gaussian. Thus the exact finite Gaussian regression formula does not give an exact Gaussian posterior for those classification models.

$$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))_{i,j};$$
repeated indices are allowed.

Given a real Gaussian process $f=(f_t)_{t\in\mathcal X}$ with mean
$m(t)=\mathbb E[f_t]$ and covariance
$k(s,t)=\mathbb E[(f_s-m(s))(f_t-m(t))]$, and a nonempty finite training list
$X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n$ in $\mathcal X$, define $f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$ and
$m_X=(m(x_i))_{i=1}^n$. For a centered Gaussian noise vector
$\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ with symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance
$R$ that is independent of $f$, define the observation vector
$Y=f_X+\varepsilon$ and the matrix
$A_X=K_{XX}+R$.

For a nonempty finite test list $X_*=(x_j^*)_{j=1}^p$ in $\mathcal X$,
define the latent test
vector $f_*=f_{X_*}$. If a centered Gaussian vector
$\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ with symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance
$R_*$ is independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$, define the noisy test
vector $Y_*=f_*+\eta_*$.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, $m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, and
$k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ a symmetric kernel whose every
finite Gram quadratic form on points of $\mathcal X$ is nonnegative. Let
$f=(f_t)_{t\in\mathcal X}$ be the canonical Gaussian process with
$m(t)=\mathbb E[f_t]$ and
$k(s,t)=\mathbb E[(f_s-m(s))(f_t-m(t))]$. For finite ordered lists
$A=(a_i)_{i=1}^r$ and $B=(b_j)_{j=1}^s$ in $\mathcal X$, set
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))$; repetitions are allowed. Take
$X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n\in\mathcal X^n$ and
$X_*=(x_j^*)_{j=1}^p\in\mathcal X^p$ with $n,p\ge1$, and write
$m_X=(m(x_i))$, $m_*=(m(x_j^*))$, $f_X=(f_{x_i})$, and
$f_*=(f_{x_j^*})$. Let $\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of $f$,
where $R$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\varepsilon$ and
$A_X=K_{XX}+R$. Suppose $A_X$ is positive definite. Then for every
$y\in\mathbb R^n$ the conditional law of $f_*$ given $Y=y$ has mean
$$m_*+K_{*X}A_X^{-1}(y-m_X)$$
and covariance
$$K_{**}-K_{*X}A_X^{-1}K_{X*}.$$
This covariance is positive semidefinite and may be singular. If
$\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ is independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$, where
$R_*$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, then the conditional law of
$f_*+\eta_*$ has the same mean and covariance with $R_*$ added. The displayed
kernel is defined for every $y$, although regular conditional versions are
determined only $P_Y$-almost surely.

In the finite observation model, let $K=K_{XX}$ and let $R$ be symmetric and
positive semidefinite. Then $A=K+R$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
Its ordinary inverse exists if and only if $A$ is positive definite,
equivalently if and only if all singular values of $A$ are positive. Thus the
standard inverse formulas are defined exactly under $A\succ0$; no ordinary
inverse formula applies when $A$ is singular.

derivations.claim: For any finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_r\in T$ and real $c_i$, the Gram form for $k(s,t)=\phi(s)\phi(t)$ is $(\sum_i c_i\phi(t_i))^2\ge0$. Thus [A1, F0] supplies the canonical prior. At $X=(a,b)$ this gives $K=vv^T=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$. Therefore $A_X=I_2+vv^T$ satisfies $c^TA_Xc=\lVert c\rVert^2+(v^Tc)^2>0$ for every nonzero $c$; [F3] confirms the inverse branch applies.

The identity $(I_2+vv^T)v=(1+v^Tv)v=6v$ gives $A_X^{-1}v=v/6$, and hence $A_X^{-1}y=A_X^{-1}(1,0)^T=(5/6,-1/3)^T$. Since $K=v v^T$, $K A_X^{-1}y=v(v^TA_X^{-1}y)=v/6$. Formula [F2] therefore gives the stated posterior mean.

Also $K A_X^{-1}K=v(v^TA_X^{-1}v)v^T=(5/6)vv^T$, because $v^TA_X^{-1}v=5/6$. Thus the posterior covariance is $K-(5/6)K=K/6$. The nonzero vector $(2,-1)^T$ is annihilated by $K/6$, while $K/6\ne0$, so this covariance is singular.

risk_review.notes: Read complete Example and Verification 1.1–3.1 and all six suppliers. Feature Gram form is a square, including repeated indices. v=(1,2), K=vv^T and A=I2+vv^T are correctly formed; A is positive definite although K is singular. Inverse is [[5,-2],[-2,2]]/6, so A^-1 y=(5/6,-1/3), A^-1 v=v/6, mean v/6 and latent covariance K/6. The nonzero vector (2,-1) is a null vector while K/6 is nonzero. Positive observation noise therefore does not imply nonsingular latent prediction. AC and finite nonempty lists are explicit; no defect.
